text: Blood pressure is a measurement of the force exerted against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps blood to the body. High blood pressure, or hypertension, is present when one or both blood pressure readings are 130/80 mm Hg or higher most of the time. Blood pressure is normal when it is lower than 120/80 mm Hg most of the time. When the top number is between 120 and 129 mm Hg and the bottom number is less than 80 mm Hg, the reading is called elevated blood pressure. Stage 1 high blood pressure ranges from 130/80 to just below 140/90 mm Hg, and stage 2 high blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg or higher.

Most of the time, no cause of high blood pressure is found; this is called essential, or primary, hypertension. High blood pressure that is caused by another medical condition or by a medicine being taken is called secondary hypertension. A person is more likely to have high blood pressure if they are African American, obese, often stressed or anxious, drink too much alcohol, eat too much salt, have a family history of high blood pressure, have diabetes, or smoke. Untreated high blood pressure can lead to heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, eye problems, and other health issues, which is why regular measurement and control are important.

text: The Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure, known as JNC 7, defined four blood pressure categories for adults. Normal blood pressure is a systolic pressure below 120 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure below 80 mm Hg. Prehypertension is a systolic pressure of 120 to 139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of 80 to 89 mm Hg. Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 140 to 159 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of 90 to 99 mm Hg. Stage 2 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 160 mm Hg or greater or a diastolic pressure of 100 mm Hg or greater. Under JNC 7, therefore, hypertension begins at 140/90 mm Hg, and the 120 to 139 over 80 to 89 range is labeled prehypertension rather than hypertension.

The Eighth Joint National Committee, JNC 8, focused on treatment thresholds and goals rather than redefining the categories of blood pressure. For patients aged 60 years or older without diabetes or chronic kidney disease, the recommended goal was a blood pressure below 150/90 mm Hg. For patients aged 18 to 59 years without major comorbidities, and for patients aged 60 or older who have diabetes or chronic kidney disease, the recommended goal was below 140/90 mm Hg. This represented a more lenient systolic goal for older adults than the earlier JNC 7 goals of below 140/90 mm Hg for most patients and below 130/80 mm Hg for patients with comorbid conditions.

text: Blood pressure (BP) is the pressure of circulating blood against the walls of blood vessels. Most of this pressure results from the heart pumping blood through the circulatory system. When used without qualification, the term "blood pressure" refers to the pressure in a brachial artery of the upper arm, the standard site of measurement. Blood pressure is usually expressed in terms of the systolic pressure (the maximum pressure during one heartbeat) over the diastolic pressure (the minimum pressure between heartbeats) and is measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg), above the surrounding atmospheric pressure. The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures is known as the pulse pressure, while the average pressure during a cardiac cycle is the mean arterial pressure. Normal resting blood pressure in an adult is, according to the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology, under 120/80 mmHg, while the European Society of Cardiology places the threshold under 120/70 mmHg. Blood pressure varies over longer time periods (months to years) and shows short-term variability from moment to moment; it also differs between individuals. Values that are persistently above the normal range constitute hypertension, whereas values persistently below the normal range may indicate hypotension.

Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guideline, adult office blood pressure is classified into four categories defined by systolic and diastolic thresholds. "Normal" blood pressure is a systolic pressure less than 120 mmHg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mmHg. "Elevated" blood pressure is a systolic pressure of 120 to 129 mmHg and a diastolic pressure less than 80 mmHg. "Hypertension, Stage 1" is a systolic pressure of 130 to 139 mmHg or a diastolic pressure of 80 to 89 mmHg. "Hypertension, Stage 2" is a systolic pressure of 140 mmHg or higher, or a diastolic pressure of 90 mmHg or higher. Because the categories combine systolic and diastolic criteria, a person is placed into the higher category if either the systolic or the diastolic value meets its threshold. This 2017 classification is notably more aggressive than older schemes in lowering the systolic and diastolic values at which the diagnostic label "hypertension" is applied, moving the threshold for stage 1 hypertension down to 130/80 mmHg.

Blood pressure classification differs substantially among the major guideline bodies, and Wikipedia's comparison of office-measurement categories highlights this heterogeneity. Under the ACC/AHA (2017) scheme, readings of 130-139 systolic with diastolic below 80 mmHg are labelled "Elevated," and readings of 130-139/80-89 mmHg are labelled "Hypertension, stage 1." The European Society of Cardiology (ESC, 2024) groups 120-139/70-89 mmHg together as "Elevated," rather than separating the 130-139 range as hypertension. The ESH/ISH (2023) framework designates 130-139/85-89 mmHg as "High normal" rather than as a hypertensive stage. For office measurements of 140/90 mmHg or above, all of these guidelines agree on a diagnosis of hypertension, but the ACC/AHA standard is distinctly more aggressive in lowering the thresholds at which elevated pressure is named as hypertension and treatment is considered. This divergence means that a single individual with an office reading of, for example, 135/85 mmHg could be classified as having stage 1 hypertension by ACC/AHA, "elevated" pressure by the ESC, and "high normal" pressure by the ESH/ISH.

The concept of "prehypertension" was introduced by the U.S. Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee (JNC 7) to describe blood pressure readings above optimal but below the diagnostic threshold for hypertension. The 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines subsequently reclassified this borderline range. Under ACC/AHA, "elevated blood pressure" is defined as a systolic pressure from 120 to 129 mmHg together with a diastolic pressure under 80 mmHg, and readings of 130/80 mmHg or higher are classified as hypertension. European practice uses different terminology and cut-points: the European Society of Hypertension designates "high normal blood pressure" as a systolic pressure from 130 to 139 mmHg and a diastolic pressure of 85 to 89 mmHg, and considers readings greater than or equal to 140/90 mmHg to be hypertension. The ACC/AHA approach therefore uses lower thresholds, creating a narrower "elevated" range and an earlier hypertension classification than the European standards, so that the same measurement can carry different diagnostic labels depending on which guideline is applied.

Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, is a long-term medical condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. High blood pressure usually does not cause symptoms itself, and for that reason it is often described as a "silent" condition; it is typically identified through screening or when investigating an unrelated problem. Hypertension is nonetheless a major risk factor for a range of serious outcomes, being associated with stroke, coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, peripheral arterial disease, vision loss, chronic kidney disease, and dementia. Long-standing untreated hypertension can cause organ damage. Because the diagnosis rests on repeated measurement rather than symptoms, definitions of hypertension are expressed in terms of numeric systolic and diastolic thresholds that vary between clinical guidelines. Hypertension is generally divided into primary (essential) hypertension, which has no single identifiable cause, and secondary hypertension, which is due to an identifiable underlying condition.

Hypertension is classified by cause into two broad types. About 90-95% of cases are primary, defined as high blood pressure due to non-specific lifestyle and genetic factors. Lifestyle factors that increase the risk include excess salt in the diet, excess body weight, smoking, physical inactivity, and alcohol use. The remaining 5-10% of cases are categorised as secondary hypertension, defined as high blood pressure due to a clearly identifiable cause, such as chronic kidney disease, narrowing of the kidney arteries (renal artery stenosis), an endocrine disorder, or the use of birth control pills. The distinction is clinically important because secondary hypertension may be improved or cured by treating the underlying cause, whereas primary hypertension is managed by lifestyle modification and, when needed, long-term antihypertensive medication. The predominance of primary hypertension means that in most patients no specific cause is found, and treatment is directed at controlling the blood pressure itself and reducing associated cardiovascular risk.

Essential hypertension (also called primary hypertension, or idiopathic hypertension) is a form of hypertension without an identifiable physiologic cause. It is the most common type, and the condition tends to be familial and is likely to be the consequence of an interaction between environmental and genetic factors. Although essential hypertension has no single identifiable cause, several risk factors have been identified as contributing to its development; these include genetics, race, diet, aging, obesity, alcohol consumption, renin levels, diabetes-related insulin resistance, smoking, vitamin deficiency, and lack of physical exercise. The disorder develops gradually over many years. Because a specific correctable cause cannot be pinpointed, management of essential hypertension focuses on lifestyle change and pharmacological control of blood pressure rather than on eliminating an underlying disease. Sustained essential hypertension can increase the risk of cerebral, cardiac, and renal events, so long-term control is directed at preventing these complications. In quantitative terms, essential hypertension is often cited as affecting around 85% of those with high blood pressure, with the remaining share accounted for by the various causes of secondary hypertension, so it dominates everyday clinical practice.

Secondary hypertension (or, less commonly, inessential hypertension) is a type of hypertension which has a specific and identifiable underlying primary cause. It affects only a minority of hypertensive patients, contrasting with essential hypertension, which lacks an identifiable cause. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is one of the most common causes; a substantial fraction of patients who have OSA also have co-morbid secondary hypertension. Kidney disorders are a major group of causes, including renovascular hypertension arising from obstruction of a renal artery, and renal parenchymal diseases such as polycystic kidney disease and glomerulonephritis, while chronic kidney disease frequently presents with hypertension. Endocrine disorders form another important group and include hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), Cushing's syndrome from excess glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, and hypothyroidism. Pheochromocytoma, a tumor that results in excessive secretion of norepinephrine and epinephrine, promotes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure. Coarctation of the aorta and certain medications, including NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and steroids, can also cause secondary hypertension. Unlike primary hypertension, secondary hypertension has an identifiable and often treatable underlying cause.

Secondary hypertension results from an identifiable cause, and recognising these causes is a key part of the evaluation of raised blood pressure. Kidney disease is the most common secondary cause of hypertension. Hypertension can also be caused by endocrine conditions, such as Cushing's syndrome, hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, acromegaly, Conn's syndrome or hyperaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, hyperparathyroidism, and pheochromocytoma. Other causes of secondary hypertension include obesity, sleep apnea, pregnancy, coarctation of the aorta, excessive eating of liquorice, excessive drinking of alcohol, certain prescription medicines, herbal remedies, and stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine. The breadth of this list means that when hypertension is severe, resistant to treatment, of sudden onset, or occurs in a young person, clinicians consider investigation for a secondary cause, since treating the underlying disorder may resolve or greatly improve the elevated blood pressure. Overall, secondary causes account for only a small proportion of hypertension, on the order of 5 to 10 percent of cases, which is why screening for them is targeted at higher-risk presentations rather than applied universally.

Pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure, is frequently increased in older people with hypertension. This can mean that systolic pressure is abnormally high, but diastolic pressure may be normal or low, a condition termed isolated systolic hypertension. In clinical terms, if the systolic blood pressure is elevated (greater than 140 mmHg) with a normal diastolic blood pressure (less than 90 mmHg), it is called isolated systolic hypertension, and it represents a specific type of widened, or high, pulse pressure. The condition is strongly age-related: about eighty percent of people with systolic hypertension are over the age of 65 years. Isolated systolic hypertension is therefore one of the most common blood pressure patterns seen in the elderly and is an important target of treatment despite the diastolic pressure appearing unremarkable. As a specific type of widened pulse pressure, isolated systolic hypertension reflects the gap between a high systolic value and a normal diastolic value, and its strong association with older age makes it a frequent finding when screening elderly populations.

Isolated systolic hypertension may be due to reduced compliance of the aorta with increasing age. As the large elastic arteries stiffen, they are less able to buffer the pressure wave generated when the heart contracts, so the systolic pressure rises while the diastolic pressure may remain normal or even fall. This increases the load on the ventricle and compromises coronary blood flow, eventually resulting in left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary ischemia, and heart failure. Because isolated systolic hypertension reflects arterial stiffening rather than raised peripheral resistance alone, it is particularly characteristic of older adults, in whom it is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Treatment of isolated systolic hypertension aims to lower the systolic pressure while avoiding excessive reduction of an already normal or low diastolic pressure. Left untreated, the increased load on the ventricle and reduced coronary perfusion can progress to left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary ischemia, and ultimately heart failure, which is why the systolic elevation is treated despite the reassuring diastolic reading.

White coat hypertension (WHT), also known as white coat syndrome, is a form of labile hypertension in which people exhibit a blood pressure level above the normal range in a clinical setting, although they do not exhibit it in other settings. It is believed that the phenomenon is due to anxiety experienced during a clinic visit, so that a patient's daytime ambulatory blood pressure, which reflects typical daily stress levels, serves as a more accurate reference point than the reading taken in the office. The contrasting phenomenon is masked hypertension, whereby a patient's blood pressure is above the normal range during daily living but not in a clinic setting. Recognising white coat hypertension is important because relying on office readings alone could lead to over-diagnosis and unnecessary treatment, whereas masked hypertension could be missed if only clinic measurements are used. White coat hypertension is regarded as a form of labile hypertension, and its recognition has contributed to changes in diagnostic protocols that place greater weight on out-of-office measurements before a lasting diagnosis is made.

Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and patient self-measurement using a home blood pressure monitoring device is being increasingly used to differentiate those with white coat hypertension or experiencing the white coat effect from those with chronic hypertension. Comparative data support home measurement in this role: a 2006 study of 98 patients showed that home blood pressure monitoring is as accurate as a 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in determining blood pressure levels. The prevalence of white coat hypertension can be substantial; in one Turkish study of 438 consecutive patients, 38% were normotensive, 43% had white coat hypertension, 2% had masked hypertension, and 15% had sustained hypertension. In terms of outcomes, individuals with white coat hypertension have lower morbidity than patients with sustained hypertension, but higher morbidity than the clinically normotensive, indicating that the condition is not entirely benign and warrants follow-up. These prevalence figures underline why guidelines increasingly favour confirming raised clinic readings with home or ambulatory monitoring before committing a patient to lifelong drug treatment.

Masked hypertension (MH) is the contrasting phenomenon to white coat hypertension, whereby a patient's blood pressure is above the normal range during daily living but not in a clinic setting. Because the office reading appears normal, the diagnosis depends on out-of-office measurement: ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and patient self-measurement using a home blood pressure monitoring device are increasingly used to identify it, and home monitoring has been found to be as accurate as 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in determining blood pressure levels. In a Turkish study of 438 consecutive patients, 2% had masked hypertension, alongside 43% with white coat hypertension and 15% with sustained hypertension. Masked hypertension is clinically important because affected patients carry cardiovascular risk that would be overlooked if only clinic measurements were relied upon, so guidelines encourage out-of-office measurement to detect it. Compared with people who are normotensive both in and out of the clinic, those with masked hypertension face raised cardiovascular risk, so the reliance on out-of-office measurement is intended to avoid falsely reassuring office readings.

Resistant hypertension is defined as high blood pressure that remains above a target level, despite being prescribed three or more antihypertensive drugs simultaneously with different mechanisms of action. Before this label is applied, apparent resistance must be distinguished from true resistance. To confirm true resistant hypertension, the drug treatment regimen should consist of optimal or best tolerated doses, and inadequate blood pressure control should be verified by out-of-office measurement methods, such as home blood pressure monitoring or 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, to exclude the white-coat effect. Medication adherence must also be confirmed and secondary causes excluded. When these factors are not properly addressed, the terms pseudoresistant or apparent resistant hypertension are proposed. Correct classification matters because it determines whether the response is to intensify therapy or to investigate for a reversible underlying cause. The requirement for three or more agents with different mechanisms of action, together with confirmation of adherence and exclusion of the white-coat effect, is what separates genuinely resistant hypertension from apparent or pseudo-resistant cases.

Some common secondary causes of resistant hypertension include obstructive sleep apnea, primary aldosteronism, and renal artery stenosis, along with rarer conditions such as pheochromocytoma and coarctation of the aorta. Primary aldosteronism is especially notable: as many as one in five people with resistant hypertension have primary aldosteronism, which is a treatable and sometimes curable condition, so testing for it is an important part of the evaluation. Resistant hypertension may also result from elevated activity of the autonomic nervous system, a form sometimes termed neurogenic hypertension. Because these underlying contributors are potentially reversible, systematic assessment of secondary causes is a central step in managing patients whose blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite multiple agents. Because primary aldosteronism may be present in as many as one in five of these patients and is potentially curable, and because obstructive sleep apnea and renal artery stenosis are also common and treatable, evaluation for secondary causes can materially change management and, in some cases, resolve the resistant hypertension entirely.

A hypertensive crisis is severely elevated blood pressure, defined as a value equal to or greater than 180 mmHg systolic or 120 mmHg diastolic; the term is sometimes associated with malignant or accelerated hypertension. People experiencing a hypertensive crisis may have no symptoms, but are more likely to report headaches (in about 22% of cases) and dizziness than the general population. Additional symptoms can include visual deterioration due to retinopathy, breathlessness due to heart failure, or a general feeling of malaise. Because blood pressure at this level can cause rapid injury to organs, a hypertensive crisis is treated as a distinct clinical situation separated according to whether or not there is evidence of acute organ damage. The 180/120 mmHg threshold marks the level at which the risk of acute organ injury rises sharply, and although some people remain asymptomatic, the possibility of headache, dizziness, visual deterioration, breathlessness, or general malaise prompts urgent assessment to determine whether organ damage is occurring.

Hypertensive crises are divided into hypertensive emergency and hypertensive urgency according to the presence of acute organ injury. A hypertensive emergency occurs when there is evidence of direct damage to one or more organs as a result of severely elevated blood pressure greater than 180 mmHg systolic or 120 mmHg diastolic. In a hypertensive emergency, rapid reduction of the blood pressure is mandated to stop ongoing organ damage, typically with intravenous agents in a monitored setting. In contrast, hypertensive urgency involves severely elevated blood pressure without evidence of acute organ damage; for hypertensive urgency, the use of oral medications to lower the blood pressure gradually over 24 to 48 hours is advocated. The distinction is therefore not based on the blood pressure number alone but on whether target organs are being acutely harmed, and it directly determines the speed and route of treatment. This division into emergency and urgency therefore drives whether blood pressure is lowered rapidly with intravenous agents under close monitoring or gradually with oral medication over roughly one to two days.

In a hypertensive emergency, the acute damage caused by severely elevated blood pressure can affect several organ systems, and the pattern of injury guides urgent treatment. Potential complications include hypertensive encephalopathy, caused by brain swelling and dysfunction, which may present with headache, confusion, or visual disturbance. Chest pain can indicate heart muscle damage such as myocardial ischemia or infarction. Pulmonary edema, the swelling of lung tissue due to left ventricular failure, may cause severe breathlessness. Other manifestations of a hypertensive crisis include visual deterioration from retinopathy and signs of kidney involvement. Because these processes represent ongoing, active organ damage, a hypertensive emergency requires prompt, carefully controlled reduction of blood pressure rather than the gradual lowering appropriate to uncomplicated hypertension. The specific organ affected, whether the brain, heart, lungs, eyes, or kidneys, shapes both the presenting symptoms and the choice and pace of treatment, reflecting that a hypertensive emergency is defined by active organ injury rather than by the blood pressure number alone.

The auscultatory method of blood pressure measurement uses a stethoscope and a sphygmomanometer. An inflatable cuff is placed around the upper arm at roughly the same vertical height as the heart and inflated to occlude the brachial artery, after which the pressure is gradually released while the clinician listens over the artery. When blood just starts to flow in the artery, the turbulent flow creates a "whooshing" or pounding sound, the first Korotkoff sound, and the cuff pressure at this point indicates the systolic pressure. As the cuff pressure continues to fall, the sounds change and eventually disappear; the pressure at which sound disappears marks the diastolic pressure. Correct cuff size is important: undersized cuffs record too high a pressure, while oversized cuffs may yield too low a pressure, so selecting a cuff appropriate to the arm circumference is essential for an accurate reading. The auscultatory method, historically using a mercury column, remains a reference technique for office blood pressure measurement.

The oscillometric method of blood pressure measurement was first demonstrated in the nineteenth century and involves the observation of oscillations in the sphygmomanometer cuff pressure. In modern automated devices, the cuff is inflated and then deflated electronically while the instrument measures the small pressure fluctuations produced by blood pulsing through the artery. From the pattern and amplitude of these oscillations, the device calculates systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressures. The oscillometric method requires less operator skill than the auscultatory technique because it does not depend on a clinician listening for Korotkoff sounds, which makes it well suited to automated office devices, home monitors, and 24-hour ambulatory recorders. Arterial pressure is thus most commonly measured either by auscultation with a sphygmomanometer or, in automated equipment, by the oscillometric method. Because the electronic device interprets the oscillation pattern automatically, the result is less dependent on the observer, though correct cuff size and proper positioning of the arm at heart level remain important for accuracy, just as with the auscultatory technique.

Accurate home blood pressure monitoring depends on standard conditions and correct technique. A person should avoid coffee, cigarettes, or strenuous exercise for about 30 minutes before taking a reading. For 5 minutes before the reading, one should sit upright in a chair with one's feet flat on the floor and with limbs uncrossed. The cuff should be placed directly against bare skin rather than over clothing, and the same arm should be used consistently, kept relaxed and supported at the level of the heart during measurement. Following these steps reduces variability and avoids falsely high or low values. Home blood pressure monitoring is increasingly used as an out-of-office method, providing readings that better reflect a person's usual blood pressure than a single clinic measurement and helping to identify white coat and masked hypertension. By capturing multiple readings taken under consistent, relaxed conditions, home monitoring gives a fuller picture of a person's usual blood pressure than an isolated office measurement and has been found comparable to 24-hour ambulatory monitoring for this purpose.

Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) measures blood pressure at regular intervals throughout the day and night, capturing blood pressure over the course of the full 24-hour sleep-wake cycle and thereby providing data outside the clinical setting. ABPM is distinguished from two alternatives: office blood pressure measurements taken in clinical environments, and home blood pressure readings taken by patients themselves. A key advantage is that ABPM avoids the white coat hypertension effect, in which a patient's blood pressure is elevated during the examination process due to nervousness and anxiety caused by being in a clinical setting. It can also detect the reverse condition, masked hypertension, where the patient has normal blood pressure during the examination but uncontrolled blood pressure outside the clinical setting. Out-of-office measurements are highly recommended as an adjunct to office measurements by almost all hypertension organizations, reflecting the recognition that a single clinic reading may not represent a person's true blood pressure burden.

First-line medications for hypertension include thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors), and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). These classes are recommended because they have been shown to lower blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular events, and treatment is often started with one of them, or a combination, depending on patient characteristics. As of 2018, the best available evidence favors low-dose thiazide diuretics as the first-line treatment of choice for high blood pressure when drugs are necessary. Beta-blockers such as atenolol were once thought to have similar beneficial effects when used as first-line therapy for hypertension; however, a Cochrane review that included 13 trials found that the effects of beta-blockers are inferior to those of other antihypertensive medications, which is why they are generally not preferred as an initial single agent for uncomplicated hypertension. In practice, treatment may begin with a single first-line agent or a combination drawn from the thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs, chosen according to the individual patient's characteristics and coexisting conditions.

ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) inhibit the activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), an enzyme responsible for the conversion of angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor. By reducing the formation of angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors promote vasodilation and lower the secretion of aldosterone, which decreases sodium and water retention; the net effect is a fall in blood pressure. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) act on the same renin-angiotensin system but at a different point: ARBs work by antagonizing the activation of angiotensin receptors, blocking the action of angiotensin II at its receptor rather than preventing its formation. Both classes are considered first-line agents for hypertension, and they are particularly used in patients who also have conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Because they share a mechanism centred on the renin-angiotensin system, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are generally not combined with each other. This shared action on the renin-angiotensin system explains both their effectiveness in lowering blood pressure and their particular value in patients who also have diabetes or chronic kidney disease.

Calcium channel blockers block the entry of calcium into muscle cells in artery walls, resulting in the relaxation of muscle cells and vasodilation. By relaxing vascular smooth muscle, they widen the arteries and reduce peripheral vascular resistance, which lowers blood pressure. Calcium channel blockers are one of the recommended first-line drug classes for hypertension and are frequently used in older patients and, in some guidelines, as an initial choice for people of African or Caribbean descent. Thiazide diuretics act through a different mechanism: diuretics help the kidneys eliminate excess salt and water from the body's tissues and blood. This reduction in circulating volume, along with longer-term effects on the blood vessels, lowers blood pressure. Low-dose thiazide diuretics are regarded, on the best available evidence, as a first-line treatment of choice for high blood pressure when medication is required. Together, calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics act on different parts of the circulation, one relaxing the artery walls and the other reducing salt and water, which is part of why agents from different classes are often combined to control blood pressure.

Beta-blockers can block beta-1 adrenergic receptors and/or beta-2 adrenergic receptors. Those that block beta-1-adrenergic receptors prevent the binding of endogenous catecholamines such as epinephrine and norepinephrine, which ultimately reduces blood pressure through decreasing renin release and cardiac output. Beta-blockers were once regarded as broadly interchangeable with other first-line antihypertensives, but the evidence base has shifted their position in treatment. A Cochrane review that included 13 trials found that the effects of beta-blockers are inferior to those of other antihypertensive medications when used as first-line therapy for hypertension. As a result, beta-blockers are generally reserved for patients who have an additional specific indication, such as certain heart conditions, rather than being chosen as the initial agent for uncomplicated high blood pressure. By reducing renin release and cardiac output through blockade of beta-1 adrenergic receptors, beta-blockers still lower blood pressure, but the finding that their protective effects are inferior to those of other first-line agents has moved them to a more selective role in hypertension treatment.

Lifestyle factors that increase the risk of hypertension include excess salt in the diet, excess body weight, smoking, physical inactivity, and alcohol use. These are considered modifiable risk factors because they can be changed to lower blood pressure. Reducing dietary salt intake lowers blood pressure, as does weight loss, exercise training, vegetarian diets, increased dietary potassium intake, and high dietary calcium supplementation. Increasing alcohol intake is associated with higher blood pressure, but the possible roles of other factors such as caffeine consumption and vitamin D deficiency are less clear. Psychological and social factors also contribute: depression is associated with hypertension, and loneliness is also a risk factor. Because these influences are potentially reversible, lifestyle modification is a central part of both preventing and treating high blood pressure, and it is recommended for all patients regardless of whether medication is also used. The consistency of the evidence that reducing salt, losing weight, exercising, moderating alcohol, and increasing dietary potassium all lower blood pressure is why these measures form the foundation of management even before drugs are considered.

Some risk factors for hypertension cannot be modified. Blood pressure rises with aging in societies with a western diet and lifestyle, and the risk of becoming hypertensive in later life is substantial in most such societies, making age a major non-modifiable determinant. Genetic factors are also important: primary, also termed essential, hypertension results from a complex interaction of genes and environmental factors, and more than 2,000 common genetic variants with small effects on blood pressure have been identified. Family history and ethnicity likewise influence risk. These non-modifiable factors help explain why some people develop hypertension despite a healthy lifestyle and why screening becomes increasingly important with advancing age. Their presence does not remove the benefit of addressing modifiable factors, but it does mean that lifelong monitoring is prudent for people with a strong genetic or age-related predisposition. The large number of small-effect genetic variants identified helps explain why blood pressure tends to run in families and why, in populations with a western diet and lifestyle, the likelihood of developing hypertension climbs steadily with advancing age.

Hypertensive heart disease includes a number of complications of high blood pressure that affect the heart. Sustained elevated blood pressure increases the workload on the heart, and among its cardiac consequences are left ventricular hypertrophy and left ventricular remodeling, in which the muscle of the main pumping chamber thickens in response to the chronic pressure load. Chronic hypertension can also lead to coronary heart disease and accelerated atherosclerosis as the elevated pressure damages blood vessel walls over time. Additional features include diminished coronary flow reserve and silent myocardial ischemia, and eventually heart failure, including heart failure with normal left ventricular ejection fraction. The chronic stress of elevated pressure forces the heart muscle to thicken and work less efficiently, progressively impairing its pumping ability. Overall, hypertensive heart disease represents one of the most important forms of target-organ damage caused by long-standing high blood pressure. The combination of hypertrophy, reduced coronary flow reserve, and accelerated atherosclerosis links hypertensive heart disease to both ischemic events and the eventual development of heart failure.

Hypertension is a leading contributor to heart failure. By imposing a chronic pressure load on the left ventricle, high blood pressure promotes left ventricular hypertrophy and remodeling, and over time this can progress to impaired cardiac function. Hypertension increases the risk of heart failure by roughly two- to three-fold and accounts for a substantial share of all heart failure cases. The resulting heart failure may occur with a reduced ejection fraction or with a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, the latter being closely linked to the stiff, hypertrophied ventricle characteristic of long-standing hypertension. Because much of this damage develops silently before symptoms appear, control of blood pressure is one of the most effective ways to prevent the development of hypertensive heart failure. Because the raised pressure first produces a thicker, stiffer left ventricle before overt symptoms appear, hypertension is estimated to increase the risk of heart failure roughly two- to three-fold and accounts for a large share of heart failure cases in the population.

Hypertensive retinopathy is damage to the retina and retinal circulation due to high blood pressure. The changes result from damage and adaptive changes in the arterial and arteriolar circulation in response to the high blood pressure. Because the retinal vessels can be viewed directly with an ophthalmoscope, hypertensive retinopathy provides a visible window onto the vascular injury caused by hypertension elsewhere in the body. Early arteriolar changes include generalized arteriolar narrowing, focal arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, and changes in the arteriolar wall (arteriosclerosis), with appearances described as copper wire arterioles and silver wire arterioles as the process advances. More advanced retinal lesions encompass microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages and flame hemorrhages, ischemic changes such as cotton wool spots, hard exudates, and, in severe cases, swelling of the optic disc. Detecting these signs on examination of the optic fundus is one of the classic ways in which long-standing untreated hypertension is recognised. These fundoscopic changes are graded by severity and correlate with the degree of systemic vascular damage, so the eye examination can indicate how advanced the hypertensive injury has become elsewhere in the body.

Hypertensive retinopathy is commonly described using the Keith-Wagener-Barker grading system, which classifies the severity of retinal changes seen on ophthalmoscopy. Grade 1 shows vascular attenuation, that is, generalized narrowing of the retinal arterioles. Grade 2 comprises the features of grade 1 together with arteriovenous nicking, or "AV nipping," where a vein appears compressed as an arteriole crosses it. Grade 3 adds retinal edema, cotton wool spots, and flame-shaped hemorrhages to the earlier changes. Grade 4 is the most severe, adding optic disc edema (papilledema) and a macular star of exudates. The grade carries prognostic significance: historical data showed that about 70% of those with grade 1 retinopathy were alive after 3 years, whereas only 6% of those with grade 4 survived, illustrating how the retinal findings mirror the severity of systemic hypertensive damage. The progression from simple arteriolar narrowing in grade 1 through arteriovenous nicking, hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots to optic disc swelling in grade 4 provides a graded, directly visible index of how far hypertensive vascular injury has advanced.

Hypertensive kidney disease is a medical condition referring to damage to the kidney due to chronic high blood pressure. It occurs where chronic high blood pressure causes damage to kidney tissue; this includes the small blood vessels, glomeruli, kidney tubules, and interstitial tissues. The tissue hardens and thickens, a process known as nephrosclerosis. The narrowing of the blood vessels means less blood is going to the tissue, and so less oxygen is reaching the tissue, resulting in tissue death (ischemia). Clinically, the condition manifests as hypertensive nephrosclerosis, with sclerosis referring to the stiffening of renal components. Signs and symptoms of chronic kidney disease, including loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, itching, sleepiness or confusion, weight loss, and an unpleasant taste in the mouth, may develop as kidney function declines. Hypertensive kidney disease is thus a form of target-organ damage in which sustained high blood pressure progressively injures the filtering apparatus of the kidney.

Hypertensive nephropathy refers to kidney failure that can be attributed to a history of hypertension. It is a chronic condition, and it is a serious risk factor for the development of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). The underlying injury is nephrosclerosis, in which chronic high blood pressure damages the small blood vessels, glomeruli, tubules, and interstitial tissue of the kidney, causing the tissue to harden and thicken and reducing blood and oxygen supply so that tissue death occurs. Over years, this progressive damage lowers the kidney's filtering capacity and can culminate in kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplantation. Because hypertension is both a cause and a consequence of kidney disease, control of blood pressure is central to slowing the progression toward end-stage kidney disease. The characteristic lesion is nephrosclerosis, a hardening and thickening of the small renal vessels and glomeruli that reduces blood and oxygen supply, and over years this steadily lowers the filtering capacity of the kidney until failure may develop.

Long-standing untreated hypertension can cause organ damage, with signs such as changes in the optic fundus seen by ophthalmoscopy, chronic kidney disease, and thickening of the heart muscle. Beyond these, hypertension increases the risk of a wide range of cardiovascular and other diseases. It is associated with ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, and other cardiovascular diseases, including heart failure, aortic aneurysms, diffuse atherosclerosis, chronic kidney disease, and atrial fibrillation. It is also linked to vision loss and to dementia. Because these complications accumulate silently over years while blood pressure remains elevated, the rationale for detecting and treating hypertension is largely to prevent this target-organ damage rather than to relieve symptoms, since high blood pressure usually does not cause symptoms itself. The breadth of associated conditions, spanning the heart, brain, kidneys, large arteries, eyes, and cognition, is why hypertension is considered one of the most important modifiable contributors to cardiovascular disease and premature death worldwide.

Blood pressure treatment targets differ across the major hypertension guidelines, and the general management goal has traditionally been to achieve a blood pressure below a range of about 140/90 mmHg to 160/100 mmHg depending on the patient. The JNC 8 guidance supports a low-dose thiazide-based diuretic as first-line treatment for general populations, with a recommended target of less than 150/90 mmHg for adults aged 60 and over. The 2017 ACC/AHA guidance, informed by the SPRINT trial, recommends targeting a systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg rather than 140 mmHg in appropriate candidates, though this more aggressive target is associated with increased adverse events. These differences mean that the same patient could be assigned different blood pressure goals depending on which guideline a clinician follows. The gap between an older goal of below about 140/90 mmHg and the more intensive systolic targets supported by newer trials is one of the clearest sources of disagreement in how tightly blood pressure should be controlled.

Guideline recommendations on antihypertensive drug choice and targets vary by region and patient group. NICE (UK) guidance emphasizes calcium channel blockers for those over 55 years of age or of African or Caribbean descent, and for elderly patients sets targets of clinic readings below 150/90 mmHg, or below 145/85 mmHg on ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring. The ESC/ESH (European) recommendations advise a systolic blood pressure target of 130-139 mmHg if tolerated for patients aged 65 and over, reflecting consideration of the side-effect burden in older populations. The primary variation across guidelines concerns systolic targets: traditional guidance recommends around 140 mmHg, while newer evidence supports 120-130 mmHg ranges for higher-risk patients, though with trade-offs regarding tolerability. This lack of a single universal target is one of the clearest examples of legitimate heterogeneity between hypertension standards. NICE, ESC/ESH, and the American guidelines each set somewhat different clinic and out-of-office targets and favour different initial drug choices, so the recommended goal depends heavily on the patient's age, risk profile, and region.

Guidelines vary slightly in how they define the upper limit of normal blood pressure. According to the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology, normal resting blood pressure in an adult is under 120/80 mmHg. The European Society of Cardiology sets the threshold at under 120/70 mmHg, using a lower diastolic cut-point. Generally, pressures over 90/60 mmHg are considered acceptable, though low blood pressure is typically harmless unless it produces symptoms. The existence of two slightly different "normal" definitions illustrates how even the boundary of normal blood pressure is not fixed across expert bodies. In practice this means that a diastolic value in the low-to-mid 70s might be counted as fully normal under one guideline while sitting at the very edge of normal under another. This small but real difference between the American under-120/80 mmHg definition and the European under-120/70 mmHg definition is a further example of how expert bodies do not fully agree even on where normal blood pressure ends.

Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, is a chronic medical condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries is higher than it should be. Blood pressure is written as two numbers, the systolic pressure over the diastolic pressure. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80. A reading of 120-129 mmHg systolic with a diastolic below 80 is considered elevated blood pressure. Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 130-139 or a diastolic pressure of 80-89. Stage 2 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 140 or higher, or a diastolic pressure of 90 or higher. High blood pressure often causes no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, which is why regular checks are important. Over time, high blood pressure can damage the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes if it is not controlled. Because it can be detected only by measuring blood pressure, and because the numbers decide which category a person falls into, regular checks are the main way that high blood pressure is found before it causes harm.

There are two main types of high blood pressure. Primary hypertension develops gradually over time without another disease causing it, and it accounts for about 90-95% of cases. Secondary hypertension results from an underlying condition and represents only about 5-10% of cases. Secondary hypertension can stem from sleep apnea, kidney problems, adrenal tumors, thyroid issues, birth defects in blood vessels, certain medications, and illegal drugs. General risk factors that make high blood pressure more likely include age, race, family history, obesity, physical inactivity, tobacco use, excessive salt intake, inadequate potassium, alcohol consumption, stress, kidney disease, and diabetes. Knowing whether hypertension is primary or secondary matters, because secondary hypertension can sometimes be cured by treating the condition that is causing it. Because primary hypertension has no single cause and cannot simply be cured, it is usually managed for life with healthy habits and, when needed, medicine, whereas finding a treatable cause of secondary hypertension can sometimes bring blood pressure back to normal.

Treatment for high blood pressure usually begins with lifestyle changes. Recommended changes include losing weight, exercising regularly, reducing salt intake, limiting alcohol, eating more fruits and vegetables, reducing stress, and getting adequate rest. When lifestyle changes are not enough to control blood pressure, doctors prescribe medicines. These include diuretics, which increase urination to get rid of extra fluid, and beta blockers, which slow the heart rate. Other medicines relax or widen the blood vessels. People often need to take blood pressure medicine for a long time, and sometimes more than one medicine is needed to reach a safe blood pressure. Because high blood pressure can return if treatment stops, ongoing monitoring and continued treatment are usually necessary. Doctors often start with one medicine and add others if blood pressure stays high, and they keep checking the readings over time to make sure the treatment is working and to adjust it, since keeping blood pressure in a safe range lowers the chance of serious problems.

text: The Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure (JNC 7) classifies blood pressure in adults on the basis of the average of two or more properly measured, seated readings taken on each of two or more office visits. Normal blood pressure is a systolic pressure below 120 mm Hg and a diastolic pressure below 80 mm Hg. Prehypertension is a systolic pressure of 120 to 139 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of 80 to 89 mm Hg. Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic pressure of 140 to 159 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of 90 to 99 mm Hg. Stage 2 hypertension is a systolic pressure of at least 160 mm Hg or a diastolic pressure of at least 100 mm Hg. When systolic and diastolic pressures fall into different categories, the higher category is used to classify the individual's blood pressure status. This framework sets the diagnostic threshold for hypertension at 140/90 mm Hg.

text: According to JNC 7, prehypertension is not a disease category. Rather, it is a designation chosen to identify individuals at high risk of developing hypertension, so that both patients and clinicians are alerted to this risk and are encouraged to intervene and prevent or delay the disease from developing. Individuals who are prehypertensive are not candidates for drug therapy on the basis of their blood pressure level alone and should be firmly and unambiguously advised to practise lifestyle modification in order to reduce their risk of developing hypertension in the future. The goal for individuals with prehypertension and no compelling indications is to lower blood pressure to normal levels through lifestyle changes and to prevent the progressive rise in pressure over time. This designation contrasts with the later 2017 ACC/AHA guideline, which eliminated the prehypertension category and instead introduced an elevated blood pressure category (120 to 129 mm Hg systolic with diastolic below 80 mm Hg) while reclassifying much of the former prehypertensive range as stage 1 hypertension.

text: The World Health Organization defines hypertension, also called high blood pressure, as the condition in which the pressure in the blood vessels is too high, at 140/90 mm Hg or higher. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the first, systolic, number represents the pressure in the blood vessels when the heart contracts or beats, while the second, diastolic, number represents the pressure in the vessels when the heart rests between beats. Hypertension is diagnosed if, when it is measured on two different days, the systolic blood pressure readings on both days are at least 140 mm Hg and/or the diastolic blood pressure readings on both days are at least 90 mm Hg. High blood pressure is common but can be serious if it is not treated. Most people with hypertension do not feel any symptoms, so the only reliable way to know is to have the blood pressure checked. This WHO diagnostic threshold of 140/90 mm Hg is consistent with the European ESC/ESH and JNC definitions and is higher than the 130/80 mm Hg threshold used by the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline.

text: A central and deliberate disagreement exists between the American and European hypertension guidelines over where the diagnostic threshold should sit. The 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines redefine hypertension as blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or higher and classify hypertension into two stages, whereas the ESC/ESH guidelines continue the conventional definition of 140/90 mm Hg or higher to classify a patient as hypertensive and provide three grades. Before diagnosing a patient as hypertensive, the ACC/AHA guideline adds a new category of elevated blood pressure when systolic pressure is 120 to 129 mm Hg and diastolic pressure is below 80 mm Hg, whereas the ESC guideline uses the terminology high-normal when systolic pressure is 130 to 139 mm Hg and diastolic pressure is 85 to 89 mm Hg. Thus the threshold for labelling a patient hypertensive and classifying him or her into the various categories of hypertension is higher in the European document than in the ACC/AHA document. In practical terms, a person with a blood pressure of 132/82 mm Hg would be diagnosed with stage 1 hypertension under ACC/AHA but merely regarded as having high-normal blood pressure under ESC/ESH.

text: Isolated systolic hypertension is the predominant form of hypertension in the older adult population. The traditional diagnostic criterion specifies a systolic blood pressure above 140 mm Hg paired with a diastolic pressure below 90 mm Hg, although the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline redefined the systolic threshold downward, so that a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg now qualifies as hypertension across age groups. Isolated systolic hypertension in most cases develops as a result of reduced elasticity of the arterial system. Age-related processes drive this decline: increased deposition of calcium and collagen within arterial walls reduces vessel compliance and produces an unfavourable wall-to-lumen ratio. These stiffened vessels accelerate pulse-wave velocity, elevating systolic pressure while paradoxically lowering diastolic pressure, which widens the pulse pressure. Chronic diseases similarly accelerate calcium and collagen buildup and fibrotic vessel remodelling. Population data show that approximately 30 percent of persons aged 60 years and older have untreated isolated systolic hypertension, compared with about 6 percent in adults aged 40 to 50 years, making it an important target for screening and treatment in the elderly.

text: Resistant hypertension is a high-risk phenotype characterised by blood pressure readings that remain at or above 130/80 mm Hg despite maximally tolerated therapy with three antihypertensive agents of different classes, one of which is a diuretic, or by controlled blood pressure that requires four or more medications to maintain. Establishing the diagnosis requires confirming adherence to therapy and excluding a white-coat effect, so that apparent resistance is not simply the result of office blood pressure being above goal while out-of-office blood pressure is at or below target. Secondary causes of hypertension, such as primary aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease, are disproportionately common in patients with resistant hypertension and should be actively sought. Because these patients are exposed to prolonged and poorly controlled pressure elevation, they are at heightened risk of target-organ damage, including left ventricular hypertrophy and both benign and malignant arteriolar nephrosclerosis. Management combines optimisation of drug therapy, frequently with the addition of a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and attention to lifestyle factors and adherence.

text: The World Health Organization groups the risk factors for hypertension into modifiable and non-modifiable categories. Modifiable risk factors include unhealthy diets, such as excessive salt consumption and a diet high in saturated fat and trans fats with a low intake of fruits and vegetables, physical inactivity, consumption of tobacco and alcohol, and being overweight or obese. Air pollution is also recognised as a significant environmental contributor. Because these factors can be altered, they are the principal targets of lifestyle interventions aimed at preventing or controlling high blood pressure. Non-modifiable risk factors include a family history of hypertension, age over 65 years, and co-existing diseases such as diabetes or kidney disease. The distinction matters for public health strategy: population-level measures such as salt reduction, tobacco control, and promotion of physical activity address modifiable risk, whereas awareness of non-modifiable risk factors helps identify individuals who warrant more frequent blood pressure screening. The combination of a high prevalence and a largely asymptomatic course makes control of modifiable risk factors a cornerstone of hypertension prevention.

The World Health Organization notes that most people with hypertension do not feel any symptoms, which is why high blood pressure is often called a silent condition and why the only reliable way to detect it is to have the blood pressure measured. When blood pressure is very high, however, people may experience symptoms including severe headaches, chest pain, dizziness, difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, blurred vision or other vision changes, anxiety, confusion, a buzzing in the ears, nosebleeds, and abnormal heart rhythm. The presence of such symptoms in the setting of markedly elevated blood pressure may signal a hypertensive crisis requiring urgent assessment. Because the condition is usually asymptomatic in its earlier stages, the WHO stresses routine screening so that hypertension can be detected and treated before it causes serious damage to the heart, brain, kidneys, and other organs. This asymptomatic natural history is the main reason that guidelines emphasise measurement-based diagnosis rather than reliance on how a person feels.

The World Health Organization describes several serious complications of untreated or poorly controlled hypertension, which collectively represent target-organ damage. Hypertension can cause serious damage to the heart, producing chest pain, also called angina, heart attack when an artery supplying the heart is blocked, heart failure when the heart cannot pump enough blood, and irregular heartbeat that can lead to sudden death. Hypertension can also burst or block the arteries that supply blood and oxygen to the brain, causing a stroke. In addition, high blood pressure can cause kidney damage that leads to kidney failure. These consequences arise because sustained pressure elevation damages the walls of arteries throughout the body, promoting atherosclerosis and injuring the small vessels of the heart, brain, and kidneys. Because the damage accumulates silently over years, the WHO emphasises early detection and sustained control of blood pressure as the means to prevent these outcomes. The organisation frames hypertension as a leading cause of premature death worldwide precisely because of this burden of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and renal disease.

text: Antihypertensive medications are grouped into several major classes, of which the most important and widely used are thiazide-type diuretics, calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), and beta blockers. Contemporary guidelines generally recommend thiazide-type diuretics, calcium channel blockers, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line options for initial treatment of hypertension, with the choice among them influenced by the patient's age, ethnicity, and comorbid conditions. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are particularly favoured for people with chronic kidney disease or heart failure, while beta blockers are reserved as a first-line choice mainly for patients with a compelling indication such as a history of ischaemic heart disease or certain arrhythmias. Because many patients require more than one agent to reach target blood pressure, combinations that pair drugs with complementary mechanisms, for example a renin-angiotensin system blocker with a calcium channel blocker or a diuretic, are commonly used. Selecting the optimal regimen therefore depends on the individual's overall health circumstances rather than on blood pressure level alone.

Thiazide-type diuretics lower blood pressure by inhibiting sodium transport in the distal tubule of the kidney through blockade of the sodium-chloride cotransporter, which promotes excretion of sodium and water. They cause an initial volume depletion associated with decreased cardiac output, but this effect recovers within about six to eight weeks of starting treatment through a reverse-autoregulation mechanism, while the blood pressure remains controlled; thiazides also produce a modest vasodilatory effect whose mechanism is still unclear. Because thiazides can acutely activate the renin-angiotensin system, adding an ACE inhibitor or an ARB may enhance their blood-pressure-lowering effect. Among the available agents, chlorthalidone is often preferred over hydrochlorothiazide, since switching from hydrochlorothiazide to chlorthalidone can decrease systolic blood pressure by an additional seven to eight mm Hg owing to its greater potency and longer duration of action. Recognised adverse effects of thiazides include disturbances of potassium and magnesium, elevated uric acid that may precipitate gout, and elevations of blood glucose. Thiazide-type diuretics remain a guideline-recommended first-line class for the initial treatment of hypertension.

ACE inhibitors are a class of antihypertensive drugs that lower blood pressure by inhibiting the angiotensin-converting enzyme, the enzyme responsible for converting angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor. By reducing angiotensin II production, ACE inhibitors decrease vasoconstriction and lower systemic vascular resistance, and they simultaneously increase levels of bradykinin by inhibiting its degradation, which contributes further to vasodilation. This dual action lowers mean arterial pressure as well as systolic and diastolic pressure in both hypertensive and normotensive subjects. ACE inhibitors are especially useful in patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetes with proteinuria, or heart failure, where they confer benefits beyond blood pressure lowering. Characteristic adverse effects follow from their mechanism: the increase in bradykinin can cause a persistent dry cough and, less commonly, angioedema with swelling of the face and neck, while reduced angiotensin II activity can raise serum potassium and cause light-headedness. Because of the risk of fetal harm, ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. They are considered a first-line class for the initial treatment of hypertension.

Angiotensin II receptor blockers, commonly abbreviated ARBs, lower blood pressure by blocking the binding of angiotensin II to the angiotensin type 1 (AT1) receptor, thereby inhibiting the vasoconstrictor and sodium-retaining effects of angiotensin II. They act at the receptor rather than at the converting enzyme, which distinguishes them mechanistically from ACE inhibitors, and because they do not increase bradykinin levels they are much less likely to cause the dry cough associated with ACE inhibitors. ARBs are frequently used as an alternative in patients who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, and like ACE inhibitors they are favoured in patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetic kidney disease, or heart failure. Common adverse effects include elevation of serum potassium and dizziness, and, as with ACE inhibitors, they are contraindicated in pregnancy because of the risk of fetal harm. Combining an ARB with an ACE inhibitor is generally avoided owing to increased risk of renal impairment and hyperkalaemia without added benefit. ARBs are a guideline-recommended first-line class for the treatment of hypertension.

Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure by inhibiting the entry of calcium ions into cells through L-type voltage-gated calcium channels located in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle. The class is divided into two main subgroups with different clinical profiles. Dihydropyridines, such as amlodipine and nifedipine, act predominantly on vascular smooth muscle to cause peripheral arterial vasodilation, which reduces systemic vascular resistance and lowers blood pressure. Non-dihydropyridines, such as verapamil and diltiazem, exert greater effects on the heart, producing negative inotropic effects and slowing cardiac contractility and conduction through the atrioventricular node. Because dihydropyridines primarily relax vascular smooth muscle, their typical adverse effects include headache, dizziness, flushing, and peripheral oedema, particularly swelling of the lower extremities, whereas non-dihydropyridines may cause bradycardia and should be used cautiously with beta blockers or in patients with reduced cardiac function. Calcium channel blockers are a guideline-recommended first-line class for the treatment of hypertension and are frequently combined with a renin-angiotensin system blocker.

Beta blockers lower blood pressure by inhibiting catecholamines such as adrenaline and noradrenaline from binding to beta-adrenergic receptors, principally the beta-1 receptors of the heart. The resulting negative inotropic and chronotropic effects decrease heart rate, myocardial contractility, and myocardial oxygen consumption, and beta blockade also reduces renin release from the kidney, contributing to the antihypertensive effect. Beta blockers are no longer regarded as first-line therapy for uncomplicated hypertension in most guidelines, but they remain first-line choices for patients who have a compelling cardiac indication, such as a history of myocardial infarction, ischaemic heart disease, certain arrhythmias, or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Agents differ in selectivity: beta-1 selective (cardioselective) drugs act more specifically on the heart, whereas non-selective agents also block beta-2 receptors and may cause bronchoconstriction, making them less suitable for people with asthma. Abrupt discontinuation of a beta blocker can provoke rebound tachycardia and hypertension, so the dose is normally tapered.

text: The 2021 WHO guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults provides evidence-based recommendations on when to initiate drug treatment, which drug classes to use, target blood pressure to be achieved for control, recommended intervals for follow-up, and which cadres within the health system can initiate and manage treatment. The recommendations target the general adult, non-pregnant hypertensive population. Importantly, the guideline deliberately limits its scope: it does not address the measurement of blood pressure, the diagnosis of hypertension, or the management of hypertensive crisis, all of which are covered by other documents. This focus reflects the guideline's public-health purpose of standardising and simplifying pharmacological management so that hypertension can be treated effectively across diverse and often resource-limited health systems. By specifying preferred first-line drug classes and encouraging the use of combination therapy and simplified treatment protocols, the WHO aims to improve rates of blood pressure control worldwide, given that hypertension is a leading modifiable cause of cardiovascular disease and premature death.

text: Isolated systolic hypertension develops chiefly through age-related stiffening of the large arteries. With advancing age, and accelerated by chronic disease, increased deposition of calcium and collagen within the arterial wall reduces the elasticity and compliance of vessels such as the aorta. Stiffer arteries cannot buffer the pulse generated by each heartbeat as effectively, so the pressure wave travels faster and is reflected back to the central aorta earlier in the cardiac cycle. The result is a rise in systolic pressure and, because the stiffened arteries store less elastic energy to sustain pressure during diastole, a fall or lack of rise in diastolic pressure, producing the widened pulse pressure characteristic of the condition. This mechanism explains why isolated systolic hypertension, defined by a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or more with a diastolic pressure below 90 mm Hg, predominates in older adults, and why the Framingham Heart Study found that individuals aged 65 with currently normal pressures still faced roughly a 90 percent lifetime risk of eventually developing hypertension. It is an important and treatable contributor to cardiovascular risk in the elderly.

text: A hypertensive crisis denotes a severe, acute elevation of blood pressure, generally a systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or higher and/or a diastolic pressure of 120 mm Hg or higher, and it is divided into two categories according to whether acute target-organ damage is present. A hypertensive urgency is a severe blood pressure elevation without evidence of acute or progressive target-organ dysfunction, and it is typically managed by gradual reduction of blood pressure over hours to days with oral medication. A hypertensive emergency is a severe elevation accompanied by acute or ongoing target-organ damage, such as encephalopathy, intracerebral hemorrhage, acute heart failure or pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection, or, in pregnancy, eclampsia; it requires immediate but controlled reduction of blood pressure, usually with intravenous agents in a monitored setting. Distinguishing urgency from emergency is essential because the pace and route of treatment differ, and overly rapid lowering of pressure can itself cause harm by reducing perfusion to vital organs.

text: Blood pressure is reported as two numbers reflecting the phases of the cardiac cycle. The first and higher number, the systolic pressure, is the pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts and ejects blood, whereas the second and lower number, the diastolic pressure, is the pressure in the arteries when the heart relaxes and fills between beats. Both numbers are measured in millimetres of mercury (mm Hg) and are written as systolic over diastolic, for example 120/80 mm Hg. Hypertension classifications assign thresholds to each component, and when the systolic and diastolic values fall into different categories the higher category is used to classify the individual. Isolated systolic hypertension refers to an elevated systolic pressure with a normal diastolic pressure and is common in older adults, whereas isolated diastolic hypertension, elevation of the diastolic pressure alone, tends to occur in younger people. The difference between the systolic and diastolic values is the pulse pressure, which widens as large arteries stiffen with age and is itself a marker of cardiovascular risk.

text: Comparisons of the American and European approaches emphasise that the difference in hypertension thresholds is a difference in labelling and treatment thresholds rather than in the underlying continuous relationship between blood pressure and risk. Both the ACC/AHA and the ESC/ESH frameworks agree that cardiovascular risk rises progressively with blood pressure from levels well within the so-called normal range. The 2017 ACC/AHA guideline responded by lowering the diagnostic threshold to 130/80 mm Hg, thereby classifying more of the population as hypertensive and prompting earlier lifestyle and, in higher-risk patients, drug intervention. The ESC/ESH and later ESH guidelines chose to retain the 140/90 mm Hg diagnostic threshold, labelling the 130 to 139 / 85 to 89 mm Hg band high-normal, while still recommending intervention in that band for selected very-high-risk patients. The 2023 ESH update narrowed the practical gap by adopting treatment targets close to 130/80 mm Hg for many patients, so that although the definitions of hypertension still differ, the guidelines now converge more closely on how aggressively blood pressure should ultimately be lowered.

text: Primary aldosteronism is one of the most common and important causes of secondary hypertension. It results from autonomous overproduction of the hormone aldosterone by the adrenal glands, most often due to a solitary aldosterone-producing adenoma or to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Excess aldosterone promotes sodium and water retention and potassium excretion by the kidney, raising blood pressure and, in some patients, producing hypokalaemia, although many affected individuals have normal potassium levels. Primary aldosteronism should be suspected in patients with resistant hypertension, hypertension accompanied by spontaneous or diuretic-induced low potassium, hypertension with an adrenal mass, or early-onset hypertension or stroke. Screening is typically performed by measuring the plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, with confirmatory testing and adrenal imaging where appropriate. Recognising primary aldosteronism matters because targeted treatment, whether surgical removal of an adenoma or a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone, can markedly improve blood pressure control and reduce the excess cardiovascular and renal risk associated with aldosterone excess, which exceeds that expected from the blood pressure elevation alone.

text: The 2018 ESC/ESH guidelines summarise their key messages on when and how to treat. Lifestyle modification, comprising dietary salt restriction, moderation of alcohol, increased consumption of vegetables and fruit, weight control, regular physical activity, and smoking cessation, is recommended for all patients, both to lower blood pressure and to reduce cardiovascular risk. For most patients, drug treatment is recommended to begin with a combination of two agents, preferably in a single-pill combination, rather than with a single drug, because combination therapy achieves control faster and improves adherence. The preferred combinations pair a renin-angiotensin system blocker, an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, with either a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic; beta blockers are reserved for specific indications. Treatment is intensified stepwise to a three-drug combination if control is not achieved, and the addition of spironolactone is advised for resistant hypertension. This emphasis on early combination therapy and simplified single-pill regimens marked a notable shift from earlier stepped-care approaches that began with monotherapy.
